pun_style: Cornish dialect wordplay or occupation-winking surnames; 'dreckly' (Cornish for 'sometime soon / vaguely later') is already a canonical Cornish folk-word usable as a given name pun; witness puns should echo Cornish mining or fishing vocabulary with a gentle double meaning (e.g. a surface worker who 'surfaces' information, a housekeeper who 'keeps' secrets)
notes: Cornwall 1907 sits within the Edwardian era. Mine ownership used the 'Cost Book' system: partners were called 'Adventurers'; the working manager/accountant was the 'Purser'; the underground foreman was 'Cap'n'. Surnames are authentically Cornish (Pol-, Tre-, Nan-, Ros-, Pen-, Bos- prefixes common). The pilchard festival (seine-fishing celebration) ran late summer in coastal and near-coastal parishes. A stranded outsider physician would plausibly be German or Central European given Edwardian medical tourism and spa culture. Keep authentic Cornish surnames; do not anglicise or modernise. 'Wheal' (meaning 'mine workings') in the mine name is correct period Cornish usage.
